chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ubaydullah al-Dahqan, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Aban ibn Taghlib, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messiah (peace be upon him) used to say: 'The one who refrains from treating the wound of the wounded is inevitably a partner to the one who inflicted the wound. This is because the injurer intended the destruction of the wounded, and the one who refrains from treating him did not desire his healing. So if he did not desire his healing, he has undesirably desired his destruction. Similarly, do not narrate wisdom to those unworthy of it, lest they be ignorant of you, and do not withhold it from those worthy of it, lest you be sinful. Let each of you be like a treating physician: if he sees a place for his medicine, he applies it; otherwise, he withholds.'

key_terms.الْجَارِحِ: The one who inflicts the wound

ai.seo_question: What is the ethical principle regarding sharing wisdom and knowledge in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) employs the medical analogy of the Messiah to define the precise etiquette of *hikmah* (wisdom), warning that withholding it from the worthy incurs sin while bestowing it on the unworthy causes ignorance. This teaching underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on *taqsim* (distribution) of knowledge, requiring the scholar to discern the recipient's capacity and readiness, much like a physician applying specific remedies to specific ailments. It highlights the moral responsibility of the knowledgeable to preserve the integrity of wisdom by avoiding both neglect and misuse.
